headline: All 14 findings survive in mechanism; 8 needed corrections and none argues for removing a feature. Read under the owner's clarification, production's counts are the scheduler, builds, crawlers and the team's own testing, so today's cost is small: the listed app statements total about 39 minutes of database time in 78 days, and several counts are lower bounds because the statements are younger than the 78 days (the job ledger is about 15 days old). What matters before opening is shape, not seconds. Three shapes will grow with stores and shoppers: (1) work every store pays per tick whether it changed anything or not: the five-minute dispatcher starts 78 jobs at once on 5 connections, several loop over every site (knowledge, media, AI month sums) or hash every store's products, and the cookie scan's "who is due" query scans its table twice per open site each minute (measured: 22 table scans a call with about 11 sites); (2) reads that cannot use the store index because store_id is written "is not distinct from" (122 places; re-checked with EXPLAIN), so they scan all stores' rows; (3) about 20 cached reads per cold page frame, several of them one read per feature for every store whether it uses the feature or not, with a cache that lives in one function instance. The most expensive app read still fetches every published page whole to find one page or a few titles. Fixing these before opening is cheapest: no real data, mechanical changes, days of work each.

clean: No finding in this dimension rests on a feature being unused. Where the auditor argued from an empty table (bonus expiry, cookie notes, integration deliveries, interface translations) I kept only the running cost and dropped the rest.

src/db/client.ts: one pool per instance (max 5, idle 5 s) attached to Vercel's lifecycle, node-postgres chosen for the transaction pooler with the reason written down (D37), no named prepared statements anywhere.
Statement and lock limits are the role's (15 s, 5 s) and a longer one is taken with set local inside a transaction (longerTimeout, client.ts:89-92), never a plain set through the pooler.

Transactions around single reads are rare: 12 read-only by their text among the 296 the scan could parse (391 by rg), each with a reason (a timeout raised for one report, an advisory lock held for a run).
Counting by loading rows is rare: 6 heuristic hits in 1,648 selects; counts are done with count(*) in SQL.
The read replica (replicaDb, client.ts:105-110) is built but off, used by one module (analytics-totals.ts), and costs nothing while READ_DATABASE_URL is unset.
publishedPageNames (pages.ts:713-735) pulls titles out of the JSON in SQL instead of fetching documents: the right shape, and the model for DQ-2.
Queues are claimed with for update skip locked (integrations.ts:1033-1039, cookie-scans.ts:78-83), so overlapping runs do not double-send.

Several dispatcher jobs already ask only for stores where the feature is set up (staff-alerts.ts:1018-1020 joins staff_alert_settings where summary <> 'off'). The chat agent is off by default (chat_agents.enabled default false), so the knowledge job's cost follows the stores that switch it on.

bonus_expire_due and the VAT-label midnight check are one set-based statement a tick each (2.1 ms and 7.3 ms a call): the right shape for a job over all stores, not waste. The auditor listed them under DQ-5; I took them out.

getStore() reads one wide row per store and is cached per store (stores.ts:231-277): one statement in place of many small ones. It is not oversize for its job; the auditor listed it under DQ-10 and I took it out.
The admin's session, account and membership reads are wrapped in React cache() (auth.ts:121, 215, 354, 407), and cart, checkout and order share one read per request through perRequest().

status_checks is pruned at 91 days (status.ts:265, STATUS_DAYS = 90 in src/lib/status.ts:17). The statistics file's note 'never pruned' is wrong: 20,547 rows is about 12 days of 6 checks every 5 minutes, and the table levels off near 157,000 rows.

The proxy's two store reads are kept 10 s per instance (redirect-resolve.ts:203-232, house-switch.ts:31-43). They are single-row reads. They will grow with shopper requests after opening (at most one per store per instance per 10 s), which is cost following use.

media.url has a unique index and thumbnail_url an index (baseline_3_rules.sql:2884, 9796), so the alt-text lookup in media-alts.ts:34-38 can use them once the table is large; today's sequential scans of media are the planner's choice at 699 rows.

findings.title: Nine routes are called every minute whether or not there is work, and one of their questions grows with the number of stores
findings.evidence: pg_cron schedules nine jobs with '* * * * *' (baseline_4:93-103), each a net.http_post that also reads the cron secret from Vault. Production: 352,514 calls, 3,974 s, 11.3 ms each. Each run does its polling without first asking whether anything waits. theme-shots reads every published theme with its whole snapshot, the theme contents, the showcase stores and the stored queue, updates expired claims, opens a transaction with an advisory lock to claim, then prunes (theme-shots.ts:330-342); production shows 35,101 such theme reads against a theme_shots table of 72 rows. Three callers already queue shots when a theme or demo store changes (askForThemeShots: store-starters.ts:326, design-presets.ts:825 and 2368). cookie-scan runs two updates and then a CTE over every open site with two correlated subqueries on cookie_scans written 'is not distinct from' (cookie-scans.ts:86-107), so the index on (store_id, created_at) cannot serve them: production shows 1,101,927 sequential scans of cookie_scans over 49,338 calls, 22 scans a call, 873 rows a scan. integrations claims and prunes integration_deliveries on every run (66,533 calls each). autopilot's three runners each read the pause switch (ai-pause.ts:18). pack-pictures opens a lock transaction each minute (content-packs.ts:735). Correction to the auditor: eight of the nine routes answer first and work in after() (rg after( in each route), so the ledger's 0 to 1 ms durations do not show idleness; psi-followups.md:477 lists that gap as open. The idleness shows in the row counts instead. Also corrected: cookie_scans holds 1,945 rows inside a 90-day retention, at least 21 a day, not 'about 9 scans a day'.
findings.cost: 12,960 function calls a day by the schedule, fixed whatever the store count. About 51 s of database time a day at most for the calls themselves (3,974 s over 78 days; the minute jobs are younger than that, so today's rate is higher: 13,248 calls at 11.3 ms is about 150 s a day). What grows: the cookie scan's who-is-due query does 2 table scans per open site per minute; at 1,000 open stores that is 2,000 scans of a table of about 13,000 rows each minute (estimate from the weekly scan and 90-day retention). The theme-shot polling grows with themes, not stores.
findings.who_pays: The database and the server (function invocations), every minute. No shopper or owner waits for it.
findings.fix: In order of value. (1) Cookie scan: write the two subqueries so an index serves them (c.store_id = sites.store_id for stores, the platform's null as its own branch, and an index on (store_id, finished_at) where status = 'done'), or keep a next-scan time per site; start the weekly scans from an hourly pass, keep the minute run for scans an owner asked for. (2) Theme shots: stop working out the wanted shots each minute; rely on the three askForThemeShots() callers plus a daily sweep, and let the minute run begin with one exists on theme_shots_queue_idx. (3) Move the prune deletes (integrations.ts:1062 and the platform's twin) to the daily job. (4) Optional: put an exists test in the scheduler's own SQL so no HTTP call is made when a queue is empty. It saves the function call, but it keeps each route's due test in two places (a migration and the code) and needs a heartbeat so the ledger does not read the route as late.
findings.saving: Estimate. Steps 1 to 3: the 1.1 M sequential scans of cookie_scans and 101 s of theme reads go, and the minute cost stops growing with stores. Step 4: up to 12,900 function calls a day while queues are empty; this saving shrinks once real stores give the queues work most minutes.
findings.risk: A wrong due test leaves work waiting. Keep one unconditional run every 15 minutes per route for the first weeks and compare. Step 4 has the larger risk because the test lives outside the code that does the work.
findings.already_tracked: partly: docs/audits/psi-followups.md:477 REL-06 (open) says the routes that work after answering are not recorded in the job ledger. No step covers the polling itself.
findings.verify_note: Opened the migration, all nine routes, theme-shots.ts, cookie-scans.ts, integrations.ts, ai-pause.ts, content-packs.ts and cron-runs.ts. The schedule and the statements hold. Changed: (a) the ledger-duration evidence is wrong for the eight routes that answer before working; (b) the cookie-scan count per day; (c) the saving, which is a fixed and small database cost today and shrinks with use, so I moved the weight to the one query that grows with stores (22 scans a call measured from production's own counters); (d) the SQL gate in pg_cron is now optional, last. Not in this fix: pg_cron's own run log (the cron schema is 564 MB) is not shrunk by any of this, since pg_cron logs a row per run either way.

findings.title: Every published page is read whole to find one page or a few titles
findings.evidence: listPublishedPages() selects id, slug, published (the whole document) and two dates for every published page of an owner, parses each with zod, then looks up library alt texts for every picture on every page (withPageAlts, with the URL list sent twice). It has 35 call sites (rg gives 37 lines; one is the definition and one a comment). At least 11 then do .find() for one id (front page, products page, role page, legal pages, checkout terms, account pages, the chat's page), and the menus read only titles: the platform's header and footer load every page and every article whole to build a map of id, slug and title (platform-navigation.ts:138-146); a store's footer loads them all to print up to five legal titles (legal-links.ts:24-29). Production: 79,778 calls, 781 s, 2,334,038 rows, 29 rows a call: the most expensive app statement, 33% of the listed app time. publishedPageNames (pages.ts:713) already shows the slim shape.
findings.cost: 781 s in 78 days, 9.8 ms a call, on the team's demo stores. Estimate: about 90 KB a call on disk (29 rows at about 3 KB), more as JSON on the wire, parsed each time. After opening, the size of a call follows one store's own page count (a blog with 300 articles sends 300 documents for one listing or one sitemap), and the number of calls follows cold renders across all stores, because the cache is per instance.
findings.who_pays: The server on every cold render of a page's frame; the database; a visitor waits for it on the first view after a deploy or on a cold instance.
findings.fix: Split it in two cached reads under the same tag. (1) publishedPageIndex(owner, type): id, slug, title and translated titles, markets, the search and AI flags, the two dates, taken with JSON operators in SQL, no document. (2) publishedPageById(owner, id): one document with its alt texts. Move the callers that find one id to (2) and the menus, legal links, sitemaps, robots and generateStaticParams to (1).
findings.saving: Estimate: most of the 781 s (rows shrink from whole documents to a few short columns, or to one row), the parse of every document per call, and the alt lookup for pages not being drawn. The saving per call grows with a store's content.
findings.risk: A caller that silently needed another field of the content; the types will show it, since content leaves the index type. A cold page then makes two small reads (index and one document) where it made one large one.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 3.9, Open, is the same idea for products: 'Stop reading the whole catalogue for one page')
findings.verify_note: Opened pages.ts:640-740, platform-navigation.ts:135-153, legal-links.ts, media-alts.ts and listed every call site with rg. The statement, the 29 rows a call and the .find() pattern hold. One small number fixed: 35 call sites, not 37. Added what the clarification asks: the 29 rows are demo content; the cost per call will follow each real store's page and article count, and calls follow cold renders times stores. The case does not rest on anything being unused.

findings.title: "Where is this picture used" scans every page's text for each picture, and the job re-checks every picture daily
findings.evidence: mediaUses() joins each picture to every page of the site and tests position(m.url in pg.draft::text) and the same on published, so both documents of every page are cast to text per picture; it does the same over entries, menus, saved parts, theme looks and settings in 12 union branches (media-library.ts:321-381). Production: 1,831 calls at 145 ms, and other shapes 43 at 925 ms, 198 at 133 ms, 205 at 66 ms, 776 at 47 ms: about 382 s in all, the second most expensive app statement. The five-minute media job calls it for every picture whose vector is older than a day, 'so what uses an item is kept current' (media-library.ts:797-799, 810, 815), 128 pictures a run, then only moves the date on unchanged ones (822-828): media_embeddings shows 13,414 updates on 468 rows, about 29 daily re-stamps of each. The job loops over every site with media (860-874).
findings.cost: About 382 s in 78 days on 699 pictures. It grows with pictures times pages times page size per store, every day, for every store with media and an AI connection, whether or not anything changed. Estimate: a store with 2,000 pictures and 100 pages of 50 KB scans about 20 GB of text a day.
findings.who_pays: The database, daily per picture, driven by the five-minute dispatcher; an owner opening the media library (two calls per page of the library).
findings.fix: Step 1 (S): in embedMedia re-check a picture only when something that can hold a picture changed since the vector's date (one max(updated_at) over the site's pages, products, menus and entries), not once a day. Step 2 (M): keep uses in a table media_uses(media_id, source, ref_id) written when a page, product, menu, entry or theme is saved (pageImageUrls() already lists a page's pictures) and read it in the library, the embeddings and the alt-text job; run today's query once a night to reconcile.
findings.saving: Estimate: at least 80% of the 382 s and nearly all 13,414 re-stamps after step 1; the library's read becomes an index lookup after step 2. The larger gain is that the daily cost stops growing with every store's library.
findings.risk: A writer that forgets to record a use leaves 'Used in' stale until the nightly reconcile. The list of places is already written in one comment (media-compress.ts:205-206).
findings.verify_note: Opened media-library.ts:300-395 and 770-876 and the three other callers. Re-added the shapes: 266 + 40 + 26 + 14 + 36 = 382 s. The daily re-check is by design (the comment says so); the fix keeps its purpose. Nothing here rests on an unused feature: the cost is per store with pictures.

findings.title: Each request for an AI connection sums the store's whole month of AI usage
findings.evidence: aiFor() has 92 call sites in 65 files (rg). For a store on the platform's key whose plan has a limit it calls aiRoomLeft(), which sums every ai_usage row of the month with a lateral price lookup per row and a euro conversion per day (usage-sql.ts:48-57). The one-minute memo (limits.ts:122, 139-144) lives in one function instance and ticks are five minutes apart, so it helps only within one run. The daily totals already exist (usage-meter.ts:45 writes ai_cost_micros per store and day). docs/capacity.md:610-612 describes month keys as the month's daily rows plus today's live count; the code sums the whole month live instead. Production: 6,782 calls at 37 ms and 1,732 at 57 ms, about 352 s, the third most expensive app statement, on 19,104 rows; the statement text there is the older shape, before the euro conversion.
findings.cost: About 352 s in 78 days; 37 to 57 ms in front of AI features and of each job that asks per store. It grows with a store's usage through the month and with the number of stores the five-minute jobs ask for.
findings.who_pays: The database; a shopper or owner waiting for an AI answer; each five-minute job that asks per store.
findings.fix: Do what storage_bytes already does at limits.ts:145-153 and what capacity.md describes: month to date = the daily totals in store_usage_daily plus today's rows only. Re-measure the month when a model's price is added for past dates. marketing_emails (limits.ts:135-136) has the same whole-month live count and takes the same fix.
findings.saving: Estimate: about 90% of the 352 s (one day's rows instead of a month's), and the cost stops growing through the month.
findings.risk: Past days are as good as the nightly measure. A price added later for an unpriced model must trigger a re-measure, or the limit reads low.
findings.already_tracked: not as a step. docs/capacity.md:610-612 already describes the intended shape (daily rows plus today's live count); the code does not follow it.
findings.verify_note: Opened ai.ts, limits.ts, usage-sql.ts, ai-price-sql.ts and capacity.md. Counted aiFor call sites (92). The mechanism holds. Added two things the auditor missed: the plan in capacity.md already asks for the fix's shape, and production's statement is an older text than today's code, so today's cost per call is at least as high.

findings.title: The five-minute dispatcher starts 78 jobs at once on 5 connections, and several redo work on every tick that grows with the number of stores
findings.evidence: runJobs() starts 78 jobs with Promise.all (cron-runs.ts:117; I counted the keys of the object in the route), then 5 more run in turn; with the route's own that is 84 ledger upserts a tick (production: 457,349 + 107,700 calls, 84 s). The pool holds 5 connections and a caller waits at most 5 s for one (client.ts:68-70; pg-pool rejects a waiter with 'timeout exceeded when trying to connect'). Jobs that redo work on every tick whatever changed: embeddings computes an md5 over title, terms and description of every active product translation of every store on the platform's AI (embeddings.ts:31-45; 10,201 calls, 148 s) and calls commerce.store_is_active() per row, a SQL function with a SET clause, which Postgres cannot inline (69 uses in 44 files); product saves already refresh their store's vectors (products/actions.ts:118 and four more callers). invoices calls two issuing functions for each store with a waiting order on every tick for up to 120 days, with no backoff (9,909 calls each, 167 s); its store list has limit 50 and no order by (invoice-issue.ts:70-96), so with more than 50 such stores some may never get a turn. knowledge, media and alt texts loop over sites (DQ-6, DQ-3). Taken out of the auditor's list: bonus_expire_due and the VAT-label check are one set-based statement a tick each, which is the right shape.
findings.cost: Today small: the ledger writes are 0.15 ms each, and the dispatcher's own run was 1.3 s. The jobs' recorded times sum to about 12.5 s because 78 jobs queue for 5 connections. What grows with stores: the embeddings hash (rows = all stores' active products times languages, every five minutes), the per-site loops, and the wait for a connection. When a waiter passes 5 s the job fails; that is a risk, not something the statistics show yet.
findings.who_pays: The database and one function every five minutes. Later: owners, when a job that serves them fails on a connect timeout.
findings.fix: (a) Give each job a cadence (prunes daily, trials hourly) and run only the due ones, a few at a time, so the pool is not queued 78 deep. (b) Embeddings: keep the refresh on save, run the full hash check nightly, and join stores instead of calling store_is_active() per row. (c) Invoices: a next-try time with backoff, a try at once when the seller's details are saved, and an order by on the store list. (d) Not worth doing: one batched ledger write. It saves about 12 ms of database time a tick and would lose every job's record when the function dies mid-run, which is what the ledger exists to show.
findings.saving: Estimate: most of 148 s (embeddings) and 167 s (invoices) at today's size. The real gain is that the tick's work stops growing with every store's catalogue and that a slow job no longer starves the other 77 of connections.
findings.risk: A job with too long a cadence or a wrong due test runs late. cron_jobs already records every run, so lateness shows on the platform home.
findings.already_tracked: no (psi-followups REL-06, done, built the ledger and runJobs; it set no cadence or budget)
findings.verify_note: Opened the route, cron-runs.ts, client.ts, pg-pool, embeddings.ts, invoice-issue.ts, bonus.ts:540-563, vat-admin.ts:350-376 and the function's definition. Changed: 78 jobs run at once, not 84 (5 follow in turn; 84 is the ledger rows). Removed bonus and VAT labels as examples: the auditor's case for bonus leaned on empty tables, and both are a single cheap statement a tick. Dropped the batched-ledger fix (tiny saving, real loss). store_is_active is used 69 times in 44 files, not 67 in 43. Added the invoice list's limit without order. The 5 s failure is a risk I could not show in production.

findings.title: The knowledge job reads every page whole every five minutes and re-cuts pages that have no text, forever
findings.evidence: For every site with its chat agent on, syncPageKnowledge() selects every published page and article with its whole published document (knowledge.ts:169-175; three statement shapes in production: 2,571 + 17,955 + 3,608 calls; the first returns 40 rows a call at 16 ms). It compares versions in code. A page whose text cuts to no passages (cutPassages returns [] at lib/knowledge.ts:65) has no chunk, so its stored version is null, never matches (knowledge.ts:186), and replacePassages() opens a transaction, deletes nothing and inserts nothing, on every tick. Production: 91,200 calls of delete from knowledge_chunks where page_id = $1 deleted 782 rows in all; that is 42% of the 216,877 transactions. Around it the job runs two reads for the site's languages, the blogs, the entries, a delete of dropped passages, an AI connection read and a vector pass, per site, in a loop (296-312).
findings.cost: 91,200 empty transactions (273,600 round trips: begin, delete, commit). Estimate: about 200 KB of page documents sent to the function each tick for the platform's site alone (40 rows at about 5 KB). After opening it is paid per store with the chat agent on (off by default): its whole published content and about eight statements every five minutes, one site after another in one function.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher function, every five minutes, for each site that uses the chat agent.
findings.fix: Keep what was cut in a small table knowledge_sources(page_id or entry_id, version, path), written also when there are no passages. Choose the pages to cut in SQL (published_at newer than the kept version, or the path changed) and fetch the document only for those. Call it from publishing a page and keep the job as an hourly net.
findings.saving: Measured count: 91,200 transactions and their round trips go to zero. Estimate: the whole-document read happens only when something was published, so the job's cost per store per tick drops to one small statement.
findings.risk: Low. A missed publish is caught by the hourly run.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/rules/storefront.md:407-411 states that the five-minute cron cuts pages published anew; the fix keeps it as the net)
findings.verify_note: Opened knowledge.ts:155-320 and lib/knowledge.ts:63-66 and followed the null version through the comparison at line 186. 91,200 / 216,877 = 42%. The feature is in use on the platform's own site, and the chat agent is off by default for a store, so cost follows use; the waste is the per-tick shape, which the clarification leaves standing.

findings.title: A page's frame asks about 20 questions each time its cache is cold, some of them one per feature for every store, and the cache is cold far more often than the code assumes
findings.evidence: Next's own guide: with the default handler, on serverless 'cache entries typically don't persist across requests', and no entry carries over a deploy because the key includes the build id (use-cache.md:245-259). The repo has 85 "use cache" directives, no "use cache: remote" and no cacheHandlers. Production: statements issued from functions cached for hours ran 540 to 1,020 times a day each (lower bound), for example the cookie scan result (70,257), the cookie notes (70,278), the modal check (68,878, 121 s), platform settings (53,887), the platform's menus (69,938). The statistics cannot say how those runs split between deploys, cold instances and builds; the clone holds two days of history, 115 commits, 80 of them touching code. Reading PlatformRoot and what it calls gives about 21 statements for the platform's frame (an estimate from the code, not measured): 8 for menus and names, 4 for header and footer, 5 for the consent banner, and settings, search texts, text styles and the site store. A store's frame was not counted by the auditor; siteCookies() alone awaits 8 or 9 reads one after another for a store (site-cookies.ts:89-121). Several are one read per feature that every store pays whether it uses the feature or not: the chat agent row, the affiliate and creator settings, the recommendation settings, running A/B tests, the remembered-modal check (jsonb_path_exists over every published page of the site) and the cookie notes.
findings.cost: About 20 round trips before a page's own content on each cold render (estimate: 20 to 60 ms in the same region, not measured); 121 s of database time for the modal check alone. After opening this is paid per store: with many stores each seen now and then by any one instance, a store's frame will be cold on most of the instances that serve it.
findings.who_pays: The first visitor of a store's page on a cold instance or after a deploy; the database.
findings.fix: Budget every cached read as if it were uncached. (1) Run siteCookies' independent reads with one Promise.all. (2) Fold the per-feature questions into one 'site facts' statement per store (exists subqueries for chat, tests, recommendations, referral and creator programmes, cookie notes), under the union of today's tags, so a store that uses none of them pays one read, not seven. (3) Keep the modal answer where pages are published: a stored generated column on pages (jsonb_path_exists is immutable) or a flag written by savePage. (4) Read the frame's menus and page titles from the index of DQ-2. Do not add a remote cache for these: Next's guide says it adds a network round trip per check and gains little for short reads.
findings.saving: Estimate: a cold frame goes from about 20 statements to 4 or 5; 121 s of JSON scans become a column read.
findings.risk: One larger read is refreshed by more tags. Keep the same tags on it, so nothing shows stale. Adding a stored generated column rewrites the pages table: cheap now, before opening.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 3.8 (Open) cuts round trips for cart and checkout only
findings.verify_note: Read the Next guide, platform-root.tsx, platform-navigation.ts, site-cookies.ts, page-modals.ts and the four per-feature readers. The mechanism and the call counts hold. Changed: 'every deploy empties it' is true per the guide but its share of the runs is not measurable here, and the commit counts are 27 and 88 for the two days the shallow clone holds (80 of 115 touch code), not proof of 78 days of deploys. The 21 statements are a code-read estimate for the platform's own frame. The auditor used the empty cookie_notes table as an argument; under the clarification the point is different and stronger: each feature costs every store one read per cold frame, so I added the fold into one statement.

findings.title: "is not distinct from" on store_id keeps the index from serving the hottest reads, so they scan all stores' rows
findings.evidence: 145 uses in 52 files, 122 on store_id in 40 files (rg). The ones that run most: pages.ts:71 (ownedBy, behind 79,778 calls), pages.ts:695 and 697 (67,601), pages.ts:728 and 733 (57,930), taxonomy.ts:60 (130,816), cookie-scans.ts:96 and 98 (49,338; 22 table scans a call), site-cookies.ts:46 (70,257) and :55 (70,278), page-modals.ts:23 (68,878), content-grid.ts:266, support-email.ts:267 (a join, 40,141). My own EXPLAIN on the local scratch database (PostgreSQL 16.15, generic plans, sequential scans off): with is not distinct from, store_id is only a Filter and the index is entered on type alone; with store_id = $1 or store_id is null it is an Index Cond on pages_store_slug_key. Production: pages 199,789 sequential scans reading 203 M rows, cookie_scans 1.1 M reading 962 M, terms 183,724 reading 11 M. At least six files already branch correctly (chat-agent.ts:71, media-library.ts:77, media-compress.ts:51, knowledge.ts:29, google-reviews.ts:38, instagram.ts:140).
findings.cost: Cheap per call today (1,389 pages). But each such read looks at every store's rows of that table, or every row of one type: about 1.2 billion rows read by sequential scan on these three tables in 78 days. The cost of one store's page render grows with all stores' data, which is the wrong direction once many stores exist.
findings.who_pays: The database, on every cold page render and every cron minute.
findings.fix: One shared helper, owned(storeId, column), that writes column = $1 for a store and column is null for the platform, as those six files do. Move the hot ten first. For the two joins of column to column (cookie-scans.ts:96-98, support-email.ts:267) write the store branch and the platform branch as a union. Add a scan test that fails for a new is not distinct from on store_id. This keeps the reason of the rule in docs/rules/storefront.md:179 (one query serves a store and the platform's null) and changes only how it is written. Before opening is the cheapest time: the change is mechanical and there is no real data to get wrong.
findings.saving: Estimate: the scans of pages, terms and cookie_scans become index scans of one store's rows. Little time saved at today's size; the cost stops growing with other stores' data.
findings.risk: Low. Passing null into the = branch would return nothing, which is why the helper branches in code. Each move is covered by the existing tests of that read.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/rules/storefront.md:179 is a rule that asks for the current wording for content types; the fix keeps its reason)
findings.verify_note: Re-counted with rg (145 in 52; 122 in 40) and ran my own EXPLAIN in a read-only transaction: the claim reproduces, including for a literal null. Opened the cited lines. Two small additions: six files, not four, already hold the branching helper, each its own copy; and the indexes the fix needs exist (pages_store_slug_key, terms_scope_idx, cookie_scans_store_created_idx). Nothing here rests on unused features.

findings.title: The store's slug is looked up by id again and again: the most-called statement in production
findings.evidence: select slug from commerce.stores where id = $1 ran 560,090 times, more than any other statement. It is written on 27 lines (rg; 25 are exactly this statement); 157 single-row reads of stores by id exist in 105 files. Page components know the store by id (GridPlace.owner), though the page was reached by slug. storeAndMarket() is not cached and not shared within a request, and has 11 callers. Three of them are parts drawn per request (the filterable grid, search, store parts), so there the lookup runs on every shopper request; the others sit inside cached functions and run when the cache is cold. A cached twin exists (storeSlugOf, menus.ts:283) and so does a per-request memo (perRequest, used in 4 files). The same habit for settings: aiFor() reads the provider row on every call (237,563 calls in four shapes, mostly from five-minute jobs that ask once per site), and the one-row platform_settings is read by 43 statements in 29 files.
findings.cost: At least 7,180 round trips a day today for a value that does not change. Each is a primary-key read, tiny in database time, but a round trip a page part waits for. After opening the per-request share grows with shopper traffic.
findings.who_pays: The server and the database on every render of a store page's dynamic parts; each a round trip the part waits for.
findings.fix: Carry the slug in the place the page hands its components (GridPlace gets storeSlug), so nothing is looked up. Until then make storeAndMarket() call storeSlugOf() (cached for days). Give jobs the store they already loaded instead of its id. Keep an aiFor() provider read per job run or per request.
findings.saving: Estimate: nearly all 560,090 calls, and most of the 237,563 provider reads inside one job run.
findings.risk: Low. The slug of a store does not change (menus.ts:282 says so).
findings.verify_note: Listed all 27 lines and the callers of storeAndMarket, storeOf and refreshStoreById. No job loops over stores with this statement, so page parts are the likely source, as the auditor said. Changed: I removed 'about 8 per page render'; its denominator (900 cold renders a day) was itself inferred from other counts and I could not reproduce it. Counts are 157 in 105 files by my rg (auditor 156 in 104). Added which callers run per request, since that share is the one that grows with shoppers.

findings.title: Some reads fetch whole JSON documents where a field, a card or a count is needed
findings.evidence: 61 selects name a page's document column and 14 a theme's (scan re-run). That count is not the size of the problem: many are single-page reads by id for an editor that needs the document, and one (page-modals.ts:20) tests the document in SQL. The reads where less would do, after DQ-2, DQ-6 and DQ-7: (1) theme-store.ts:137 reads every published theme with its whole snapshot to draw cards: 10,851 calls, 107,917 rows, 27 s. (2) theme-store.ts:176 reads every version's whole snapshot of a theme to write a changelog. (3) theme-shots.ts:59, the same snapshots each minute: 35,101 calls, 101 s (the same cost as in DQ-1; do not count it twice). (4) pages.ts:136, the admin's Pages list, reads draft and published of every page to show a title, a state and a thumbnail. (5) accessibility.ts:120, (6) green-claims.ts:54 and (7) store-translate.ts:125 read every page of the store; these are admin screens an owner opens, bounded by that store's content, and (5) and (6) need the content to check it in code. (8) fonts.ts:180 reads a family's whole stylesheet to pick one file name. (9) analytics-speed.ts:116 loads every speed sample of 28 days, up to 10,000 a store day, to work out a percentile in code. select * is the same habit in small: 138 in 78 files; the ones that run most are ai.ts:208 (237,563 calls) and chat-agent.ts:93 (48,492). Taken out of the auditor's list: getStore's one wide cached row per store, which replaces many small reads and is not oversize for its job.
findings.cost: 27 s for the theme cards read (the 101 s of theme-shots belongs to DQ-1); the rest is bytes and parse time on each call, not yet large. The theme reads grow with themes, not stores. The Pages list and the speed report grow with one store's content and traffic: the speed report can load up to 280,000 rows for one screen.
findings.who_pays: The server (memory and parse) and the database; an owner on the Pages list or the speed report; the theme store's visitors on a cold render.
findings.fix: Keep what cards and lists need beside the document, written when it is saved: for themes the looks, swatch and section style names at publish; for pages title, thumbnail and state as columns (generated where they can be). Write the changelog from notes kept per version. Compute the percentile in SQL (percentile_cont). Store the preload file name when a font is installed. Name the columns in the two hot select * reads. Leave the accessibility and claims screens as they are until a store's size makes them slow.
findings.saving: Estimate: the theme card read shrinks from whole themes to card facts (most of 27 s); the admin Pages list and the speed report stop growing with document size and sample count.
findings.risk: Derived columns can drift from the document. Generated columns cannot; for the others a scan test over the writers, as store-writers.scan.test.ts does for stores.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review FD7, Open in step 3.15, names the width of orders but not these reads)
findings.verify_note: Re-ran the scan (61 and 14) and opened each cited read. Changed: the title no longer presents 61 as the number of needless reads; '128 s for the two theme reads' double-counted 101 s that DQ-1 already carries; getStore is removed (a deliberate single cached read); the three admin screens are marked as cost that follows an owner's use; select * is in 78 files, not 80. SPEED_DAYS = 28 and 10,000 samples a store day are in src/lib/speed.ts:22-24, so 280,000 is a true upper bound.

findings.title: Nothing counts queries: no budget per page or per tick, and production's statement statistics are not part of any routine
findings.evidence: rg finds no query budget and no statement counter in src, e2e, scripts or docs, and pg_stat_statements is named only in the draft of this review. The ratchet (ratchet.baseline.json) holds counts of casts, suppressions, unchecked reads and writes by id alone; none is about how many statements run or how much they return. The deploy routine in CLAUDE.md asks for the security and performance advisors after a migration, not for the statement statistics. What the findings above describe was visible there for weeks: 91,200 deletes that removed 782 rows, a slug lookup called 560,090 times, 22 table scans in one scheduler query.
findings.cost: No running cost of its own. It is why the others grew unseen.
findings.who_pays: Everyone later: each new section, job and cached read adds statements with no number to hold against. The number matters more once statements multiply by stores.
findings.fix: (1) An integration test that counts statements (wrap the pool's query in the test) for one idle dispatcher tick, one idle run of each minute route, and one cold render of the demo store's front page and of the platform's home; keep the counts in the ratchet file so they may only fall. Run the idle tick against a seed of 1 and of 20 stores and fail when the count grows with stores for jobs that have no work. (2) Add to the after-deploy routine: read the 25 most-called and 25 costliest statements and explain any newcomer. (3) Extend the scan tests: no new is not distinct from on store_id (DQ-8), no new minute schedule without a due test (DQ-1).
findings.saving: Not a direct saving. It keeps DQ-1 to DQ-10 from coming back and gives each a number to check the fix against.
findings.risk: A count that wobbles makes a flaky test. Count on a seeded database with caches cold, as the existing integration tests run.
findings.already_tracked: no (code review step 4.6 'Measure, then tune', Open, is the admin audit's and names no query count)
findings.verify_note: rg for pg_stat_statements and for budget wording across src, e2e, scripts, docs and .github: only the draft review mentions it. Read the ratchet file's keys and the code review's Progress rows 3.8, 3.9, 4.6. I replaced the auditor's example of a poll on an empty table with examples that do not lean on an unused feature, and added the two-seed check, because growth with stores is what the clarification asks to guard.

findings.title: Every server instance reads the interface translations before it serves and polls them each minute
findings.evidence: register() awaits startUi() before an instance takes requests (Next's guide: register 'must complete before the server is ready to handle requests'); that runs select lang, count(*), max(updated_at) from commerce.ui_translations group by lang, then a timer repeats it every 60 s. Production: 278,393 calls, the second most-called statement. Measured locally: one statement per instance per minute (the table's scan counter moved 5 to 6 in 30 s with one next start running). Correction to the auditor: ensureUi() is called only from two email paths (shopper-emails.ts:108, notifications.ts:367); pages rely on the timer, so the timer is what keeps a long-lived instance current and cannot simply be dropped.
findings.cost: At least 3,569 round trips a day, each tiny. One round trip and a connection before a new instance serves; the first request would open that connection anyway in most cases, so the added wait is about one round trip (estimate, not measured). It grows with instances, not with stores. Once languages are translated the poll becomes a count over every translated text per instance per minute.
findings.who_pays: The first visitor served by a new instance; the database.
findings.fix: Keep the read at start and the timer, and make the poll cheaper: one version stamp row written by the translation tools and read by the poll, or a longer interval (10 minutes) while the last answer was 'no translated languages'. reloadUi() already refreshes the instance that made a change. Do not make t() wait on the database.
findings.saving: Estimate: from 1,440 polls per instance a day to 144, or the same count at a fraction of the work once the table fills. Small either way; this is a low-priority item.
findings.risk: A language translated by AI would show up to 10 minutes late on other instances with the longer interval. None with the version stamp.
findings.verify_note: Opened instrumentation.ts and ui-text.ts, listed ensureUi's callers, read Next's instrumentation guide, and measured the poll on the local database. Changed: the kind (the auditor called it speculative because the table is empty; under the clarification that is not an argument, and what remains is eager polling); the fix (dropping the timer would leave pages on long-lived instances stale, because nothing on a page path calls ensureUi); and the size of the cold-start cost, which the auditor put at tens of milliseconds without measuring. What is left is real but small.

findings.title: 341 loops hold a database call in their body; the ones that matter are jobs that loop over sites
findings.evidence: A lexical scan finds 341 loops in 183 files with an awaited database call in the loop's own body, and 5 async map callbacks (re-run: same numbers). Most run over a handful of rows by design, and their cost follows use: one insert per fee, stock hold or language when an order is placed or a product saved (checkout.ts:1081, order-insert.ts:363, products.ts:1207), one 'bought since' lookup per due cart reminder (cart-reminders.ts:353). The ones that grow with the number of stores are the dispatcher's per-site loops: knowledge.ts:301 (per site with the chat agent: a full sync, an AI connection read, a vector pass), media-library.ts:866 (per site with media: an AI connection read plus 2 to 4 statements), invoice-issue.ts:123 (two function calls per store with a waiting order), embeddings.ts:120 (per store with its own AI). Each runs its sites one after another inside one function every five minutes.
findings.cost: Per-site loops cost several round trips per site per tick, one site after another, so a tick's length grows with the stores that use the feature. The order's per-line inserts add one round trip per line while the order's transaction holds its locks.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher every five minutes; a shopper at the moment of placing an order (a few milliseconds per line).
findings.fix: Per-site jobs: one set-based statement that returns only sites with work (as storesWithDocumentWork does at invoice-issue.ts:70) and a batch for the per-site reads (one AI connection read for all sites). Inserts of several rows: one insert with many value rows, as embeddings.ts:59-70 already does. The cart reminder's lookup: a left join in the query that finds the due carts. Do the job loops with DQ-3, DQ-5 and DQ-6; leave the order's inserts to code review step 3.7.
findings.saving: Estimate: per-tick round trips of these jobs stop growing with the number of sites; an order with n lines saves about n to 2n round trips inside its transaction.
findings.risk: placeOrder is the money path: change it only with its tests, and with code review step 3.7.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 3.7 'Stage placeOrder' (Open) restructures the order's writes; D320 already made a variant save 'a few statements'
findings.verify_note: Re-ran loopscan.mjs (341 loops, 183 files, 5 maps) and opened the cited loops. They are as described. I separated the loops whose cost follows use (orders, product saves), which the clarification does not call waste, from the per-site job loops, which are the same cost already carried by DQ-3, DQ-5 and DQ-6. This finding adds little of its own; treat it as the pattern behind those three.

findings.title: 387 list reads have no limit by a heuristic count; a handful read a whole store's documents or samples
findings.evidence: Of 1,648 selects assigned to a const, 442 carry a limit and 387 return a list with no limit, no id or any() filter and no aggregate (heuristic; re-run gives the same numbers). Most are bounded by their parent (an order's lines, a store's locations). The ten that are bounded only by how much a store has: pages.ts:136 (every page with both documents, for the admin list); pages.ts:668 (DQ-2); knowledge.ts:170 (DQ-6); accessibility.ts:120; green-claims.ts:46-55 (every active product's texts and every published page); store-translate.ts:125; analytics-speed.ts:116 (up to 28 days times 10,000 samples); activity.ts:155 (select distinct action over the audit log, to fill a filter); theme-store.ts:176 (every version's snapshot); owner-assistant.ts:234-235 (select * of every message and approval of a conversation). Eight of the ten are admin screens: the cost is paid by the owner who opens them and follows that store's own size. Rows loaded only to be counted are rare: 6 hits.
findings.cost: Small today. Each of the ten returns rows in proportion to one store's whole content, so a large store makes its own screens slow. None costs anything for a store that does not open the screen, apart from the two already carried by DQ-2 and DQ-6.
findings.who_pays: An owner on the Pages list, the accessibility and claims screens and the activity filter; the server's memory.
findings.fix: Page the admin lists (the Pages list with the columns of DQ-10 and a limit, as step 1.13 will give every list). Compute in SQL what is computed from all rows (the speed percentile). Keep the audit log's distinct actions as a fixed list in code, which is where they are written. Load a conversation's newest messages first.
findings.saving: Estimate: these ten stop growing with a store's content; nothing measurable at today's sizes.
findings.risk: Paging changes what a list shows at once; it follows the shared list pattern of step 1.13.
findings.already_tracked: partly: code review step 1.13 'One way to search and page a list' (Open) covers paging admin lists; step 0.9 (Done) paged the storefront's listings
findings.verify_note: Re-ran countscan.mjs (1,648 selects, 442 with a limit, 387 without, 6 only counted) and opened the ten reads. They are as described. Under the clarification this is low priority: the cost follows an owner's use of a screen and one store's size, not the number of stores. It overlaps DQ-2, DQ-6 and DQ-10; do not count their savings again here.
